opus-5.5.text:
I think the comparison is a bit misleading if you just look at the headline numbers. When people see that some other company has much more compute, they assume it all goes to research. But a very large fraction of the compute at the big labs goes to inference, to serving products, and the research budget is spread across many different efforts, many different modalities, many product commitments. Whereas the compute we do have goes much more directly toward the research we care about.

The other thing is this: if you are doing something genuinely different, you don't necessarily need the absolute maximum scale to establish whether it works. To prove an idea is correct, you need enough compute to convince yourself, and to convince others, that there's something real there. Historically, many of the most important ideas in the field, like AlexNet and the transformer, were validated with what would now be considered very modest amounts of compute. Then scale came later and showed how far they could go.

So the question I ask is not "do we have as much as the biggest lab?" but "do we have enough to test the ideas we believe in, and to see clear signal?" And so far, I think the answer is yes. If at some point an idea works and it calls for a lot more compute to push it all the way, that's a different conversation, and it's a good problem to have.

r001.rationale: The response says headline compute comparisons are misleading because large labs spend much compute on inference and divide research across many efforts, while SSI directs more of its compute to its research.

r002.rationale: It says a genuinely different idea need not start at the largest scale; enough compute to establish that it works and show a clear signal can validate it.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the question presupposes something that I'd push back on a little, which is that the amount of compute you need to validate a research idea is comparable to the amount of compute you need to run the frontier playbook. Those are very different things.

If your plan is to do what everyone else is doing, then yes, you need what everyone else has, and more, because you're competing on the same axis. The scaling recipe is well understood at this point. Everyone knows how to do it. The differentiator becomes who has the most GPUs and the most data, and in that game we would not win and we shouldn't try.

But that's not the game. The reason SSI exists is that I think the current approach, as it's practiced, is going to hit limits, and the interesting work is in figuring out what comes after. And that kind of work, the kind where you're trying to find a different idea rather than scale a known one, has a different compute profile. You need enough compute to tell whether an idea is real. You need to be able to run experiments at a scale where the signal is not noise, where you can see whether something improves as you make it bigger. That's not nothing. It's substantial. But it's not a frontier training run.

I'd put it this way. The history of the field is that the key ideas were usually found at relatively modest scale, and then scaling made them work. The transformer was not found with a hundred thousand GPUs. What you need is the ability to see the trend. If an idea is good, you should be able to see it getting better across two or three orders of magnitude, and if you can see that, you have a strong reason to believe it continues. So the question I ask is not, do we have as much compute as the biggest labs, because the answer is obviously no. The question is, do we have enough to distinguish a good idea from a bad one with confidence. And I'm satisfied that we do, with the caveat that compute requirements are always growing and you have to keep paying attention to it.

There's also a benefit that people underrate, which is that constraint focuses you. When you can afford to try everything, you try everything, and a lot of that is waste. When you have to choose, you think harder about what to try. I'm not romanticizing scarcity. More compute is better, and we raise money so that we have what we need. But I don't think the bottleneck for the thing we're trying to do is compute. I think the bottleneck is ideas, and that's precisely why this is a bet worth making.

r001.rationale: It says validating a novel idea takes substantial but far less compute than a frontier training run, and that SSI has enough to distinguish good ideas from bad ones despite having less compute than the biggest labs.

r002.rationale: It explicitly distinguishes researching a different idea from running the frontier playbook and says validation does not require a frontier-scale training run.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is: enough compute to test which hypothesis? There are ideas where you can get a very informative answer at a relatively small scale. And there are ideas where the whole question is whether something changes when you go to a much larger scale. For those, you really do need the compute.

So I would distinguish between having enough compute to make progress in research and having enough compute to do everything a better-funded lab can do. Those are different thresholds. You don’t necessarily need to match another lab’s total budget to test a particular idea well.

But you also have to be honest about what the experiment tells you. A promising result at small scale is evidence; it isn’t proof that the approach will work at large scale. The important thing is whether you can afford the experiments that could actually change your mind.

r001.rationale: The response distinguishes research progress from matching another lab’s total budget, but does not state that SSI’s compute disadvantage is smaller than headline funding figures suggest.

r002.rationale: It says some ideas can be tested informatively at relatively small scale and that matching another lab’s total budget is not necessary to test a particular idea well.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the important question is: enough compute to test which ideas? There’s a difference between testing a research hypothesis and building the largest possible system. If an experiment can distinguish between two hypotheses at a smaller scale, you can learn something important without matching the largest labs’ budgets.

But scale can also be part of the hypothesis. In that case, a small experiment may not tell you what you need to know. So the assessment has to be concrete: what result would convince us, at what scale would we expect to see it, and can we afford that experiment? Having less compute is a real constraint. The question is whether it constrains the experiments that matter for your particular research direction.

r001.rationale: The response says less compute is a real constraint, but does not state that SSI’s disadvantage is smaller than headline funding figures suggest.

r002.rationale: It says a smaller-scale experiment can distinguish hypotheses and yield useful learning without matching the largest labs’ budgets.
